title: FIN8
summary: FIN8 is a financially motivated intrusion set that public reporting has tracked since around 2016, with a focus on hospitality, retail, and financial organisations. Its distinguishing behaviour is a preference for memory-resident execution: script interpreters such as PowerShell are used to run payloads directly, so little or no malicious file is written to disk, and code is sometimes loaded straight into a legitimate process. Public analyses describe point of sale data theft tooling, credential harvesting from the registry and local files, and living-off-the-land utilities for movement and persistence. In later activity, reporting has linked the group to ransomware deployment after access is established, which shifts the impact from quiet card theft to full operational disruption. The common misunderstanding is that fileless equals invisible; script block logging, process creation with encoded command lines, and unusual parent and child relationships all provide durable evidence even when the payload never touches storage.

beginner.definition: FIN8 is a name for a criminal group that steals payment information and, in more recent reports, also uses ransomware. Public reports describe attacks on hotels, shops, restaurants, and financial companies. They are driven by money, and they work carefully to stay hidden.
beginner.whyItMatters: This group avoids leaving bad files on disk, so ordinary file scanning may find nothing. Their activity looks like normal administration until you look closely at the process tree. Businesses in retail and hospitality are common targets because card data moves through them constantly. Detecting them early stops both stolen cards and a later encryption attack.
howItWorks: The attacker gets a first foothold through phishing, a weak password, or a service.
Built-in scripting is used to run code without saving a file to disk.
The code is placed inside a trusted running program to avoid attention.
Saved passwords and system details are collected for further access.
Payment systems are located and monitored for card information.
Administrator tools are used to spread, and ransomware may follow later.
beginner.example: Think of a stage magician who never hides an object in his pockets. Everything he needs is already on the table, in plain sight, and he simply uses what visitors expect to see. Because you search his pockets and find nothing, you assume he is honest. The table is your own system software, and the trick is using it in a way nobody expected.
takeaways: Enable detailed script logging, because it captures activity that never becomes a file.
Look at which program started which other program, not just at file names.
Treat payment systems and administrator accounts as top priority assets.

objectives: Explain how script-based, memory-resident execution avoids writing malware to disk.
Describe the telemetry that makes fileless activity still detectable.
Explain process injection into a trusted process and how to spot its effects.
Trace the path from an initial foothold to payment card data collection.
Discuss the shift from card theft to ransomware within one criminal group.
